aliases:
  - Field2d
  - Field Odometry

#stub

Synopsis

https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/dashboards/glass/field2d-widget.html

Success Criteria

  • Create a Widget on a dashboard to show the field
  • Populate the Field with your robot, and one or more targets
  • Utilize the Field to help develop a "useful feature" displayed on the Field

As a telemetry task, success is thus open ended, and should just be part of your development process; The actual feature can be anything, but a few examples we've seen before are

  • showing which of several targets your code has deemed best, and react to it
  • a path your robot is following, and where the bot is while following it
  • The current Vision targets and where your bot is when seeing them
  • A field position used as an adjustable target
  • The projected path for a selected auto
  • Inidcate proximity or zones "zones" for performing a task, such as the acceptable range for a shooting task or intaking process.

Odometry Fundamentals

Odometry is also known as Position Tracking. In FRC, this is generally regarded as knowing the position of your robot in the game field. It is most beneficial when combined with the robot to then have the robot move between positions on the field, and interact with other known positions.

Actually obtaining odometry depends on the design of the bot: Differential Drive Odometry or Swerve Odometry , and often involves vision systems via LimeLight Odometry or PhotonVision Odometry

This document is concerned with the prerequisite: Being able to actually view, compare, and validate positions using robot telemetry.

Odometry Telemetry

Telemetry for Odometry revolves around the Field2D object. Both Glass and Elastic can display the Field2D object as a game field on the dashboard, including associated robot positions and any secondary objects.

In general, Glass is the superior option for most programming tasks and development, allowing easier customization to help reduce clutter and provide clarity between objects.

The WPILib Docs are excellent at helping demonstrate many of these examples:
https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/dashboards/glass/field2d-widget.html

Pose

In Robots, a Pose represents a specific location and state of a robot's actuator. Within the context of odometry, a pose represents the robot's location on a 2D plane. In most cases, this means the location on the game field.

In order to represent such a state, we need 3 things: The X position, the Y position, and a rotation.

In WPILib, this is handled by the Pose2d object, which can be provided to and returned from many utilities interacting with the robot position, including drivetrain path planning, vision, simulation, and telemetry.

Field2D Basics

The Field2D object in WPILib contains a number of utilities for keeping tabs on odometry. It can be added with just a couple lines. 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		//We only want to send the actual Field object _once_,
		//so we often do it in the constructor. Changes will be 
		//sent automatically as the Field2d object itself is updated.
				
		//Preferred: Set the NetworkTables name explicitly, 
		//and give it a unique, descriptive name
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		
		// This form uses the default name "Field" as the key.
		// Not recommended in most cases
		//SmartDashboard.putData(field);
	}

}

This creates a blank, empty field, with your robot position, probably at (0,0) in the bottom left corner, on the blue side of the field.

Meaningfully updating the robot pose is out of scope, and differs by drivetrain type; However, the basic gist is 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	//Set up an odometry object to track our robot
	DifferentialDrivePoseEstimator odometry=new DifferentialDrivePoseEstimator(
	 /* Complex constructor parameters; not relevant*/
	)
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//Read the odometry object and set the pose. //Reference only
		field.setRobotPose(odometry.getPoseMeters());
		
		// Or, we can just set it manually for testing.
		field.setRobotPose(new Pose2d(2.7,3.1, new Rotation2d(Math.PI/2.0) ));	
	}
}

Now, when we open our Field2D widget in Glass, we'll see that our robot is at a new position. If we fully implemented our Pose Estimator object, we'd see that this provides realtime tracking of our position.

A .getRobotPose() also exists, but tends to be less useful in practice, as most classes that will interact with the Robot and Field will likely have access to the Odometry object directly.

Note, that the Field2d object we create is a unique reference, with it's own unique local data; only the NetworkTables key might have overlap when using default keys. This means if we want to properly share a Field across multiple classes, we either need to fetch the NetworkTables data and copy it over, create a single Field object in RobotContainer and pass it to, or create a DriverField object as a Singleton that can facilitate a single object.

Displaying Useful Targets

Where Field2d objects really shine is in adding supplemental information about other field objects. The utility varies by game, but it's great for showing a variety of things such as

  • Targets/objectives
  • Nearest/best target
  • Nearest game piece (detected by vision systems)

These can be done using the getObject(name) method; This grabs the named object from the field, creating it if it doesn't already exist.

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//Can provide any number of pose arguments
		field.getObject("GamePieces").setPoses(
			new Pose2d(1,1),
			new Pose2d(1,2),
			new Pose2d(1,3),
		);
		//You can also pass a single List<Pose2d> 
		//if you have a list of poses already
		
		field.getObject("BestGamePiece").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}

}

Note It's worth considering that for objects that never move, you could set objects once in the constructor, and they work fine. However, if the user accidentally moves them in the UI, it creates a visual mis-match between what the code is doing and what the user sees. As a result, it's often better to just throw it in a Periodic.

Field2d + User Input

A niche, but very useful application of field objects is to get precise driver feedback on field location data. This can be done using the following code setup:

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		//Set the pose  exactly once at boot
		field.getObject("DriverTarget").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}
	
	public Command aimAtCustomTarget(){
		return run(()->{
			var target=field.getObject("DriverTarget").getPose();
			//Do math to figure out the angle to target
			//Set your drivetrain to face the target
		};
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//No setting DriverTarget pose here!
	};
}

In this case, we take advantage of the "set once" approach in constructors; The drivers or programmers can modify the position, and then we now read it back into the code.

This can be very useful for testing to create "moving targets" to test dynamic behavior without having to drive the bot. It can also help you create "simulation" poses for testing math relating to Pose2D objects.

is especially true for simulation, as this allows you quickly test pose-related functions and makes sure that things happen how you expect.

One practical application is match-specific targets for cooperating with allies. An example is in 2024 Crescendo: a common game tactic was to "pass" rings across the field, by shooting to an open area near where your allies would be. However, since the game pieces can get stuck in/on robots, and different robots have different intakes, and each ally has different sight lines, making the ideal pass target unknown until the actual match is about to start. An adjustable target let the alliance sort it out before a match without having to change the code.

Displaying Paths

When doing path-planning for drivetrains, it's often helpful to display the full intended path, rather than a lot of individual poses. 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		//Set the pose  exactly once at boot
		field.getObject("DriverTarget").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}
	
	public Command buildAuto1(){
		var  trajectory=// Get the trajectory object from your path tool
		field.getObject("autoTrajectory").setTrajectory(trajectory);
		return run(()->{
			//draw the rest of the owl
		};
	}
	

}

In this use case, the work will likely be done inside your Auto class after selecting the appropriate one.

Code Structuring

Success Criteria

  • Set up a mock project with a nominal, standard code structure

Project should have a subsystem that

  • Is in a subsystem folder
  • Has 3 components in a (logic, Physics Simulation, Mechanism2d)
  • Has a factory method to get a control command (can be mocked up)
  • Has a trigger that indicates a mechanism state (can be mocked up based on timers)
    Has an additional sensor subsystem system that
  • Provides a trigger for a condition (can be mocked up)
    Has a controller and
    Has an Autos class to hold autos
  • With an auto chooser initialization
  • A single basic auto using subsystem and sensor

Planning your bot structure:

High level Superstructure states

Start by thinking about the broader, high level superstructure states. EG, what your bot is doing and what simpler mechanisms are involved with that.

  • Intaking game pieces
  • Scoring game pieces
  • Climbing/Performing end game

Depending on the construction you might be able to fully decouple many of these states, and even enact multiple at once.

In many systems, however, this is not true, with heavy coupling between critical subsystems. This is almost always the case for Passthrough style subsystems, which are heavily controlled on both intake and exhaust sides, complicating code.

Low Level Mechanism States

Next, think about the low level mechanisms: These should be very simplified, single actuator representations

  • Intake Rollers
  • Shooter Flywheels
  • Arm Pivot

While it's tempting to represent these as "groups", avoid the temptation and model individual motors/actuators separately if they're not rigidly linked together (as in a gearbox or shaft)

These should have very simple and consistent interfaces: You just want to set the actuator state, position, or get information from it. Broadly, the interfaces should be simplified, such as

  • setPosition/setAngle/setHeight/setVelocity
  • setVoltage (for direct output control)
  • getPosition
  • getVelocity
  • stop

Mid-Level Grouping

Now is the time to start structuring things to get from the top level generic tasks, to the lower level actuator side.

For this, look for the smallest cluster of mechanisms that independently do a useful task.

Intakes are a good example: Often you need to extend/deploy an intake along with some rollers. Since intakes are often wide, sometimes there's individual actuators on both sides, making this 3 components (left arm, right arm, rollers)

Defining your intake API helps you plan this out:

  • Intake (both arms deployed, and rollers running inward)
  • Eject (Rollers running backwards, arms might have some consideration)
  • Stop/Stow (both arms retracted, rollers stopped)

Notice, as part of this you can simply assert "When doing X, the mechanisms are doing Y". This is ideal, and what we're building toward.

Shooters are another useful grouping example, and show the value of this structural style. These have two major mechanisms (a Flywheel and a Feeder to provide it game pieces), with two critical states:

  • Shooting (Running at a goal RPM, and feeding)
  • Stopping (Idle/Stop speed and not feeding)
    However, you generally have some edge cases:
  • You don't want to feed game pieces while trying to get up to speed
  • You don't want to stop running while the feeder might be passing game pieces
    The mid level group gives you a clean place to handle this internal conflict, such that your high level group does not need to consider it.

Increasingly high level

You may need to form additional tiers as you go to fully define your goal states. Usually, you want to draw these boundary lines at places where a group of mechanisms might have specialized tasks, conditions, or groupings.

The goal of this architectural style is to streamline management, and reduce the number of high-level states you have to juggle. By letting smaller clusters manage themselves, you can usually avoid building absurdly complex State Machines , and leverage many, smaller state machines.

In general, we tend to build systems using Commands and Command groups; These are small, self contained state machines, and recognizing them as such helps with this planning.

Code Example:

For this example, we'll refer to a simple shooter bot that has an intake and a shooter system.

First, define the high level concepts 

// Somewhere in robotContainer or a superstructure class
Command shoot = Commands.parallel(
	shooter.shoot(),
);
Command intake = Commands.parallel(
	intake.intake();
);

According to this code, we're in the ideal zone where we could shoot and intake at once; Our two core states don't interact.

But importantly, these high level definitions are not really managing the details of the system, beyond ensuring that each system has what it needs to make decisions.

Now we get to probe the underpinnings of what makes those commands work.

public Shooter{
	private Flywheel flywheel = new Flywheel();
	private Feeder feeder = new Feeder();
	
	public Command shoot(){
		
		var feed = Commands.repeatingSequence(
			feeder.stop().until(flywheel.isAtTargetVelocity),
			feeder.feed().until(flywheel.isAtTargetVelocity.negate())
		);
		
		Commands.parallel(
			flywheel.setVelocity(/*goal rpm*/),
			feed	
		);
	}
}

And a similar one for our intake

public Intake{
	private IntakeArm left = new IntakeArm(/*...*/);
	private IntakeArm right = new IntakeArm(/*...*/);
	private Rollers rollers = new Rollers();
	
	public Command intake(){
		return Commands. parallel(
			left.setPosition(0),
			right.setPosition(0),
			rollers.setVelocity(500)
		)
	}
	
	public Command stow(){
		return Commands. parallel(
			left.setPosition(90),
			right.setPosition(90),
			rollers.stop()
		)
	}
	
}

The more complex one is the shooter: You can see that in this case, the Feeder actually has a small state machine: It cycles between waiting for the shooter to be up to speed, and then feeding it game pieces. But, from the perspective of the higher level control, you simply don't care: The shoot command takes care of it.

On the intake side, the high level simply doesn't care about whether there's one arm, two arms, or the like. You just tell it to intake, and it makes that happen.

This path generates a fairly consistent, streamlined flow, and works well within the idioms of WPILib and FRC in general.

Heavily coupled systems

In cases where a system is extremely tightly coupled on many different subsystems, or uninterruptible processes/transitions, this approach might fall apart, or leave you with lots of subsystems to declare with a large number of system states.

In such cases, bundle them as best as you can to reduce the overall number of global states, and then look at alternate abstractions that seem to make sense.

In some cases, instead of using Commands/Subsystems as a rigid mutex for single-owner control, you might be able to provide multiple inputs at once, and let the subsystem figure out what to do with that.

For example, a Swerve drive might have drivers trying to reposition it, but the Shooting system needs to control rotation to aim. In such cases, providing both to the drivetrain lets it add them together, and do both at once.

For some systems you might be able to provide multiple "behavior requests", and let it prioritize. For example, a indexer/feeder might have a "load new piece" and "Feed to shooter" request, and determine that the "feed to shooter" is the one to handle at that time.

Code Structuring

Roadmap:

## Understanding the tools

The Deploy folder

Odometry for basic location awareness and coordinate axes for Swerve

The Swerve Framework, YAGSL

YAGSL is a coding framework for handling a lot of swerve setup, management, and includes useful utilities for reducing code involved with

  • Configuring a swerve drive
  • Managing multiple configurations for multiple bots
  • Streamlining control+inputs and managing motors
  • Handling user input in useful ways
  • Underlying optimizations that are hard to manage in a custom codebase
    among other things.

The Yagsl Docs

Yagsl has extensive documentation and troubleshooting guides here
https://yagsl.yassrobotics.com/get-started/tutorial

However, note that these docs are written in an "ai assisted" way and will contain very confusing details, such as using old apis, unreleased apis, or simply incorrect function calls or values.

If something doesn't make sense, check with a mentor.

The Config Files

2027 Update Incoming

The Biocore season will have significant changes to swerve setup details, such as method names, json values, and meaning behind some values.

This section represents a 2026 season code sample, and shows the main concepts of creating/managing swerves. That will remain the same.

YAGSL does not track all your constants in code like we typically do for other bot-related values. Instead, it uses some external configuration in config files. These are located in a special Deploy folder, which is pushed to the robot alongside the code.

Tuning and setting up a new Swerve Drive

Bringing up a brand new serve drive is a very detail-oriented process with a lot of steps. We won't cover this here, but the Yagsl docs do a good job here. It's recommended to follow their guide when possible:

https://yagsl.yassrobotics.com/get-started/tutorial

When following this guide, it's recommended to do so on a new project dedicated for this tuning. This allows you to copy+paste the code templates during the setup that will include telemetry data specific to this process. These templates are great for this process, but structured poorly for a codebase thats going to competition!

Once you've completed that process, the resulting config files and the import loading code can be easily brought into your other codebases.

The Deploy folder

This is a special folder that gets copied to the robot alongside your new code every deploy. This allows non-java files to be kept up to date, and stored on the robot when you make changes.

Yagsl uses this to hold the config parameters, which are loaded at robot boot. You can see this on the File manager in VSCode, and once set up, will resemble something like this:

- src/main
  - deploy/
    - (robotname)/
	  - controllerproperties.json
	  - swervedrive.json
	  - modules/
        - (specific module name).json
		- (other modules...).json
		- physicalproperties.json
		- pidfproperties.json
  - java/frc/robot/
    - (your normal robot code goes here)

Because the configs are separated by the name, you can have multiple configs per project, allowing the same code to run on multiple bots without a lot of code changes.

Also, because these configs exist on the robot, that means you can use them even if you don't have them in your current project! This can be very useful for quick bringups.

It's often a good plan to leave a "gold standard', well tuned config on the robot for people who just want to work on a specific bot detail that requires a swerve drive (such as vision, testing, autos, or driver input testing), and use a different name when doing work like learning swerve tuning+creation so you don't overwrite those tested configurations.

In many cases, creating the config only needs to be done once per robot, and that configuration can be preserved as a useful team asset.

Structuring your Swerve project

The swerve system gets asked to do a lot of different jobs, and setting it up to do all those jobs can be tricky. There will be a full, commented code template later, but this part will go over some of the basics, and why it might differ from subsystems you've built so far.

Here's the initial code, and then we'll walk through some of the new parts and explain things.

// Inside SwerveDriveSubsystem.java
public class SwerveDriveSubsystem extends SubsystemBase{
  public final SwerveDrive drive;

  /** We'll discuss this in detail below */
  private final SwerveInputStream defaultInputStream;

  /**
   * Unlike most systems, our swerve needs the joystick inputs
   * we plan to use.
   */
  public SwerveDriveSubsystem(
    DoubleSupplier xThrottle,
    DoubleSupplier yThrottle, 
    DoubleSupplier rotationThrottle
  ){
    //Query the bot's Preferences table to figure out 
    // which swerve configuration we're using
    var botname = Preferences.getString("BotName", "compbot");
	
	// Try/catch is how java handles operatiosn that can fail. 
	// This can be because we can't find the config files, or
	// If the config files didn't process right.
    try {
      //Now, load that configuration.
      File swerveJsonDirectory = new File(
        Filesystem.getDeployDirectory(),
        botname
      );
    
    // and build our actual swerve drive
      drive = new SwerveParser(swerveJsonDirectory)
          .createSwerveDrive(5/*mps*/, new Pose2d(6,4,new Rotation2d));
    } catch (Exception e) {
      // In this case we cannot drive the bot.
      // Throwing this error will halt robot code, 
      // and someone must fix it before it can run,
      // but we want to provide some diagnostic info
      System.err.println("Could not find robot config for " + botname);
      throw new RuntimeException(e);
    }

    //Set up our default input stream with basic driver inputs.
    // Your exact settings may differ based on bot and driver preferences. 
    defaultInputStream = SwerveInputStream.of(
      drive, 
      xThrottle,
      yThrottle
    )
    .withControllerRotationAxis(rotationThrottle)
    .deadband(0.05)
    .scaleTranslation(0.6)
    .scaleRotation(0.4)
    .allianceRelativeControl(true)
    ;
    
    //Register our default drive command
    setDefaultCommand(driveFieldRelative(defaultInputStream));

    //Log Yagsl's default field to Glass/Elastic to visualize our position
    SmartDashboard.putData("Swerve/swervefield",drive.field);
  }

  /**
   * Run the bot with a field-oriented notation
   * @param stream The input stream we've built and are using for the bot
   * @return the command to run
   */
  public Command driveFieldRelative(SwerveInputStream stream){
    return run(()->{
	    drive.driveFieldOriented(stream.get(), Translation2d.kZero);
	})
    .withName("Drive Field Relative");
  }

  /**
   * Zero the gyro angle ; Drivers may need this to re-align the bot during matches, 
   * so it's worth putting on their controller somewhere.
   * @return
   */
  public Command zeroGyro(){
    return Commands.runOnce(drive::zeroGyro, this).withName("Zero Gyro");
  }

and in RobotContainer.java

public class RobotContainer {	
  //Our controller, if we don't have one
  private final CommandXboxController joystick = new CommandXboxController(0);

  // Our joystick inputs get passed directly to this. 
  private final SwerveDriveSubsystem swervedrive = new SwerveDriveSubsystem(
    joystick::getLeftY,
    joystick::getLeftX,
    joystick::getRightX
  );

  // ... Rest of robotcontainer
}

And now we can discuss some of the surprises

The Constructor: Creating the Swerve Object

The Bot's Name

This line is responsible for managing the bot name

    var botname = Preferences.getString("BotName", "compbot");

Preferences is just like SmartDashboard, but persists through reboots. Whatever name is set under the key (Botname) is saved, and will be loaded by this file, even if our code hasn't set it.
If that value doesn't exist, then we use the default, in this case compbot.

This lets us give a robot a specific name to map to that particular bot's swerve configuration (such as Tabi, Mjoulnir, Skipper, or CompBot). This makes it very easy to create a Swerve config that's easily loaded from projects that

In this case, we want to load whatever config that bot is named, and if we can't detect a name, we'll use "compbot". In practice, we want to default to the name our comp bot uses; This way, if we do a sudden hardware swap in a competition, but didn't have time to set the right name, we'll load the intended config.

For our personal projects, we might want to just ignore this entirely, and do a more simple name assignment. 

    //var botname = Preferences.getString("BotName", "compbot");
    var botname = "myBotName";

Try/Catch

Unlike most of our systems, the use of the "loadable configs" actually generates a "runtime" failure mode. Meaning, it's not an issue in the compiled code; It's something outside your project that the robot is interacting with. In this case, those config files.

Instead of your usual red squiggles when something goes wrong, in this case, the whole robot fails to boot, and you get "No Robot Code" on the driver station.

While Java (and other code languages) offer ways to work around it, we don't take advantage of this. Because the swerve is so key to playing the game, there's functionally nothing we can do if it doesn't load. So, we simply see the issue, emit a notice, and let the robot stop running.

This is represented by java's try/catch syntax


try{
  // Some operation that can fail 
}
catch(exception...){
 // what do to when it fails.
}

The main reasons your code will fail will be

  • Having a typo/error in your config name
  • Trying to load a config that does not exist on the robot
  • Your config is not correct/complete
  • You're loading a 2026 config in a 2027 robot
  • You're loading a 2027 config in a 2026 robot

Loading the config file + Creating a drive from it

2027 Update Incoming

The Biocore season changes the code process used to load these configs.

This section represents a 2026 season code sample, but the general routine is similar.

Inside our try block, we handle the fallable operations: Loading the config itself, and then processing it into a SwerveDrive object.

This is just as required by Yagsl . Some bots may need a couple additional configs (for certain gyro setups), and in 2027 there will likely be differences.

The only surprise is that you require a start position to create the robot. On a full bot, the chosen location is irrelevant ; A vision system or auto will re-assert your starting position. However, for now we have chosen roughly the center of the field,which will help with some debugging and initial usage.

The Field2d object

The Field2d object provides a visual reference for the Robot's position on the field. Yagsl creates this by default with useful diagnostic information, and we just need to put it on the SmartDashboard to use it.

The Zero Gyro command

The final standalone detail is the zeroGyro command. This allows the driver to set the gyro to a known heading, which lets them drive accurately.

  public Command zeroGyro(){
    return Commands.runOnce(drive::zeroGyro, this).withName("Zero Gyro");
  }

In normal operation, this command is not needed; A vision/odometry system will set the position and robot orientation.

This command is essential in case a vision system is not working, or not present, such as

  • If it's damaged or disconnected during a match
  • If there's no vision system
  • If the current room doesn't have vision targets, such as during practice

This means during practice and early season, this is a standard action when testing the bot. Driving a swerve bot without reliable control is a safety hazard.

In competition, it's a last resort in case your vision/odometry system gets damaged, and will allow drivers to continue playing the match.

As such, it's worth ensuring it works and is correctly bound to a button (usually Start or Back).

Controlling the Swerve Drive SwerveInputStream

The rest of the code we'll discuss revolves around SwerveInputStream. This is a utility class that contains helper functions for converting driver intent into swerve drive actions.

This class has a lot of options! At any given time, only a few options are relevant, and our code is based around this concept. This allows for more clearly defined splits, and prevents some issues that happen when you try to create some large, unweildly input streams.

The DriveFieldRelative Command

Most of what we'll work on next is based on this simple looking Command, which hides a few neat details:

  public Command driveFieldRelative(SwerveInputStream stream){
    return run(()->{
	    drive.driveFieldOriented(stream.get(), Translation2d.kZero);
	})
    .withName("Drive Field Relative");
  }

drive.driveFieldOriented means you're controlling based on the field and gyro, not on what direction the robot happens to be facing. So, "up" on the joystick is always means "away from the driver station", not robot oriented as in "the direction the robot considers the front" like you see on a Tank Drive style bot.

You can drive RobotOriented if you want, which has value in some special cases, such as

  • When drivers are using cameras to see "from the robot" perspective when they cannot see the robot itself
  • When doing a vision or sensor lineup where you may have relative data, but not Poses or field coordinates
  • Some particular object/field interactions may benefit from it
  • Testing the Swerve drive and modules

However, in general, Swerve bots are very difficult for drivers to control from "Robot oriented" notation, so it's advised to use it it as a special case, not as your usual operation. You can also mix-and-match using drive.DriveFieldAndRobotRelative(...) to benefit from special cases without interrupting the driver's handling.

Also note the Translation2d being provided; This represents the X+Y coordinates being used as the robot's center of rotation, in "robot oriented" space, with +X being the front of the robot.
Moving the Center of rotation can allow the driver's "rotate" command to pivot around a specified location, which might make certain robot->field interactions or auto sequences easier.

Default Swerve Input Stream

Let's loop back to our constructor, and review these parts: 

public class SwerveDriveSubsystem extends SubsystemBase{
  public final SwerveDrive drive;

  /** We'll discuss this in detail below */
  private final SwerveInputStream defaultInputStream;

  public SwerveDriveSubsystem(
    DoubleSupplier xThrottle,
    DoubleSupplier yThrottle, 
    DoubleSupplier rotationThrottle
  ){
	// ... Initialization stuff 
	
    defaultInputStream = SwerveInputStream.of(
      drive, 
      xThrottle,
      yThrottle
    )
    .withControllerRotationAxis(rotationThrottle)
    .deadband(0.05)
    .scaleTranslation(0.6)
    .scaleRotation(0.4)
    .allianceRelativeControl(true)
    ;
    
    //Register our default drive command
    setDefaultCommand(driveFieldRelative(defaultInputStream));

We see that we pass in our joystick axes in as as DoubleSuppliers . In most subsystems we avoid this, as we can just use Commands to specify action we want from that system.

However, in our case, many swerve actions will need the basic input from the human to travel the field, and we want to avoid typing it out a lot, missing settings that impact driver handling, or otherwise creating bugs.

We also, of course, need these to generate our default "just drive normally" command!

This particular "default" does the following:

	// This creates the initial entry point with the translation throttle values
    defaultInputStream = SwerveInputStream.of(
      drive, //This is our yagsl swerve object
      xThrottle,
      yThrottle
    )
    .withControllerRotationAxis(rotationThrottle)
    
    //This lets us ignore small joystick values. 
    // We normally want this at/near zero, but values near 0.05-0.10 can prevent 
    // old, driving joysticks from moving a robot accidentally
    .deadband(0.05)
    
    //These "scale" the inputs, making the bot go slower
    // You normally want these at 1 for a real bot. However, 
	// our bots and driving area are very small, so this helps 
	// keep them moving slowly and safely.
    .scaleTranslation(0.6)
    .scaleRotation(0.4)
    //Adjust our field-relative inputs based on which side of the field 
    // our drivers are on. So  "up" is away, and "right" is right.
    .allianceRelativeControl(true)
    ;

RobotContainer

Lastly, we just need to set this up so we can run it

public class RobotContainer {
  private final CommandXboxController joystick = new CommandXboxController(0);

  /* These all need to be inverted due to how joysticks present values, and
   * how our drive system expects things to be
  */
  private final SwerveDriveSubsystem swervedrive = new SwerveDriveSubsystem(
    ()-> -joystick.getLeftY(),
    ()-> -joystick.getLeftX(),
    ()-> -joystick.getRightX()
  );


  public RobotContainer(){
    configureBindings();
  }

  private void configureBindings(){
    //This resets the gyro and can be used to help get the field-oriented
    // drive to have forward/back/left/right feel correct
    joystick.back().onTrue(swervedrive.zeroGyro());
  }

Next, you may want to check out Swerve Simulation ; This helps you test your swerve code without needing the hardware.

There's a lot you can do using SwerveInputStream, which is the topic of Swerve Motion, which covers point-to-point movement, aiming, and creating custom Swerve actions.

Many good swerve interactions also rely on Swerve Odometry , which also relies on

  • Create drive commands to drive to a target point
  • Create drive commands to aim the bot at targets

Odometry is useful here!

Many advanced commands need the swerve odometry to work correctly.

While you can learn and test these bits of code, you may get unexpected results, or have difficulty validating them on hardware.

Note that using Swerve Simulation may help with this, as that provides some basic odometry and a safe environment for you.

Remixing our inputs and creating commands

Most swerve bots will want at least one alternate drive command that sets the scaleTranslation/ScaleRotation values as a "slow mode" when drivers are trying to do something precise! Or, sometimes we want to default as slow, and make a "sprint" button that unlocks full robot speed.

So, let's make one.

First, our standard structure for a new Input command will look like this:

  public Command nameOfTask(/*Any useful parameter data*/){
    var inputs = defaultInputStream
    .copy()
	/* Additional tweaks to our  input stream*/
    ;
    return driveFieldRelative(inputs);
  }

The .copy() creates a new, modifiable instance of our input stream unique to this command. We can then safely modify it without impacting our defaults or other commands.

Our entire job is now reduced to creating the adjusted input stream, an then passing it to the command we already made! Easy!

In this case, we're changing our default from slow to less slow, so let's name it Sprint. We have no parameters, so let's remove those.

  public Command sprint(){
    var inputs = defaultInputStream
    .copy()
	/* Additional tweaks to our  input stream*/
	.scaleTranslation(1)
    .scaleRotation(1)
    ;
    return driveFieldRelative(inputs);
  }

That's it! We can now bind this to a button, and we can have two different input speeds on our bot.

Aiming at A Target

A common benefit of a swerve is aiming at something other than what you're driving at. A command that handles this is created in much the same way.

  public Command aimAtTarget(Pose2d target){
    var inputs = defaultInputStream
    .copy()
    .aim(target)
    .aimWhile(true)
    ;
    
    return driveFieldRelative(inputs);
  }

Since this default still uses the joystick inputs, you still have input without having to fuss with it!

Some tasks like this change the calculation modes of a SwerveInputstream, and need to be "switched on" using a ___While(true) modifier. These switch between different ways of generating values. In this case, it changes from reading the joystick axis to control rotation, into a calculated difference between where you are, where you're facing, and where the target is.

Note: there are no PID constants in this particular case; There's some internal tricks using the individual wheel module's PID+FF values that allow it to change the rotation without having to provide them directly.

Driving To A Position

This one is slightly more complicated, and has some additional surprises. However, at the core it's the same process: 

  private Command driveToPosition(Pose2d goalPose){
    var inputs = defaultInputStream
    .copy()
    //Enable the correct mode; This one completely takes driver control away
    .driveToPoseEnabled(true)
    //This one takes several parameters
    .driveToPose( 
      ()->goalPose, 
      getTranslationPidController(),
      getRotationPIDController()
    )
    //You likely want scaling at 1 (max capability according to ProfiledPid)
    .scaleTranslation(1)
    .scaleRotation(1)
    ;
    
    return driveFieldRelative(inputs);
  }

  private ProfiledPIDController getTranslationPidController(){
    // This is in m/s and m/s/s
    var constraints = new Constraints(3, 5);
    //Our PID inputs are in meters, although output units are unclear 
    var pid = new ProfiledPIDController(2, 0, 0, constraints);
    return pid;
  }

  private ProfiledPIDController getRotationPIDController(){
    // This takes rad/s and rad/s/s , so we use a conversion from degrees
    var constraints = new Constraints(
      Units.degreesToRadians(120),
      Units.degreesToRadians(240)
    );
	//Our PID inputs are in radians, although output units are unclear 
    var pid = new ProfiledPIDController(2.5, 0, 0, constraints);
    return pid;
  }

While this could be done inside the singular command, it's a bit cleaner to break the PID generators out.

Be sure to watch your units! This is a case where we get very mixed units, as many parameters are in Meters and Radians internally. Using the Units library for conversions, and being consistent and labeling things will pay off.

Quick explainer on ProfiledPID

If you haven't been exposed to a ProfiledPID, you can treat it similarly to a raw PID controller. However, it's a bit smarter, and does three main things:

  • Reduces the accelleration when you enable it/change setpoints, so it starts smoothly
  • Constrains the speed to a maximum, defined value
  • Slows the bot down before it gets to the goal position, preventing overshoot.

As a result, it provides much better motion, is simpler to tune, works well with higher gain values, and provides more control. You typically want to set the velocity constraint at the max speed of your robot (~4-6mps). Acceleration you can just start slow and increase until your robot misbehaves, or until it can't keep up.

For comparison, you can think of a normal PID controller as having infinite acceleration and infinite velocity.

Sequencing Motions + Detecting goal conditions

Normally, sequencing motions requires the command to know that it's done, and exiting on it's own. The most useful one to sequence is our driveToPosition command. Moving to two points is very useful, and you could write whole, simple autos with it.

First, we need to figure out how to figure out if we're at a particular position. This is straightforward (you've done this math!), but uses some methods we may not have interacted with.

From your geometry class, you know that the objective is to calculate

    dx = target.x-bot.x
    dy = target.y-bot.y
    dist = sqrt(dx**2+dy**2)
    dist <= tolerance

In code, we can do that like so:

  public boolean isAtPosition(Pose2d target, Distance tolerance){
	// Get a Translation2d, representing X/Y position without the angle
	var position = drive.getPose().getTranslation();
	//We can now use a method to get the distance between those points
	// This handles the dx,dy, and sqrt
	var dist = position.getDistance(target.getTranslation())
	
	//And now we can compare it. Since the internal Pose units 
	// are meters, we have to convert our tolerance distance.
    return dist <= tolerance.in(Meters);
  }

Then, just create a variant of our driveToPosition with a decorator that exits.

  public Command driveToPosition(Pose2d goalPose, Distance tolerance){
    return driveToPosition(goalPose)
    .until( ()->isAtPosition(goalPose, tolerance) );
  }

This code isn't perfect; Try sequencing a small, square motion of 4 points, with a large tolerance (like 24in). The intended goal path isn't quite what will happen, and what you'll see is behavior like this:

Note you never got to any of your goal positions, including at the end! You'll also see it stop abruptly at each path transition, when you'd expect a smooth start and smooth stop.

What's happening is that the tolerance is cutting the motion short, before your profile can slow down and get to the goal position.

Whether this is a problem or not depends on the motion and the game. You might bump into objects, end the sequence misaligned, or not get close enough to successfully place game pieces.
On the other hand, if you're too precise a problem along the way might cause you to be just outside the tolerance, halting your sequence.

What we can do to fix both is also account for the completion of a motion by simply checking if the robot is where we need it and stopped. We need to write a new method for this. The math here doesn't need much explanation, just some conversions

  public boolean isRobotStopped(){
    var speeds = drive.getRobotVelocity();
    //These values are fairly arbitrary; You'd want to adjust them 
    // to what your got+game needs!
    //In some cases, you may want to parameterize them as part of 
    //your "isRobotStopped(...) function
    var stoppedMPS = InchesPerSecond.of(3).in(MetersPerSecond);
    var stoppedRPS = DegreesPerSecond.of(10).in(RadiansPerSecond);

	var speedxy = Math.hypot(
		speeds.vxMetersPerSecond,
		speeds.vyMetersPerSecond
	);

    return speedxy < stoppedMPS
	&& Math.abs(speeds.omegaRadiansPerSecond) < stoppedRPS ;
  }

and then add this condition to our new drive command.

  public Command driveToPosition(Pose2d goalPose, Distance tolerance){
    return driveToPosition(goalPose)
    .until( ()->isAtPosition(goalPose, tolerance) && isRobotStopped());
  }

Now the robot will very closely track your goal positions, even with a large tolerance. If unobstructed, it'll finish the motion, and won't be stopped until very close to the goal position, and will then exit, and continue the sequence.

This does a great job handling the most common obstruction: bumping into a wall near the goal. That will usually leave you stopped and within tolerance, and exit as intended. If you're too far away and had something like a robot collision, it'll continue the approach.

Other mid-movement obstructions will simply leave the bot trying to drive to the goal position, or the sequence will stall, but in the intended way. EG, if you didn't drive to your destination position, you don't want to try to score your game piece.

Other things!

You've probably noticed that there's a lot of flexibility here! There's capabilities we haven't touched on, and combinations beyond these basics.

Depending on the needs of your game/project, you can mix-and match several capabilities at once, to do things like:

  • Face a particular direction (Up/Down/Left/Right) while driving , rather than at a specific target
  • Aim at a target while while auto-driving to a field position
  • Aim at a target using the back or side of a robot

As a telemetry task, success is thus open ended, and should just be part of your development process; The actual feature can be anything, but a few examples we've seen before are

  • showing which of several targets your code has deemed best, and react to it

Odometry Fundamentals

Odometry is also known as Position Tracking. In FRC, this is generally regarded as knowing the position of your robot in the game field. It is most beneficial when combined with the robot to then have the robot move between positions on the field, and interact with other known positions.

Actually obtaining odometry depends on the design of the bot: Differential Drive Odometry or Swerve Odometry , and often involves vision systems via LimeLight Odometry or PhotonVision Odometry

This document is concerned with the prerequisite: Being able to actually view, compare, and validate positions using robot telemetry.

Odometry Telemetry

Telemetry for Odometry revolves around the Field2D object. Both Glass and Elastic can display the Field2D object as a game field on the dashboard, including associated robot positions and any secondary objects.

In general, Glass is the superior option for most programming tasks and development, allowing easier customization to help reduce clutter and provide clarity between objects.

The WPILib Docs are excellent at helping demonstrate many of these examples:
https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/dashboards/glass/field2d-widget.html

Pose

In Robots, a Pose represents a specific location and state of a robot's actuator. Within the context of odometry, a pose represents the robot's location on a 2D plane. In most cases, this means the location on the game field.

In order to represent such a state, we need 3 things: The X position, the Y position, and a rotation.

In WPILib, this is handled by the Pose2d object, which can be provided to and returned from many utilities interacting with the robot position, including drivetrain path planning, vision, simulation, and telemetry.

Field2D Basics

The Field2D object in WPILib contains a number of utilities for keeping tabs on odometry. It can be added with just a couple lines. 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		//We only want to send the actual Field object _once_,
		//so we often do it in the constructor. Changes will be 
		//sent automatically as the Field2d object itself is updated.
				
		//Preferred: Set the NetworkTables name explicitly, 
		//and give it a unique, descriptive name
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		
		// This form uses the default name "Field" as the key.
		// Not recommended in most cases
		//SmartDashboard.putData(field);
	}

}

This creates a blank, empty field, with your robot position, probably at (0,0) in the bottom left corner, on the blue side of the field.

Meaningfully updating the robot pose is out of scope, and differs by drivetrain type; However, the basic gist is 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	//Set up an odometry object to track our robot
	DifferentialDrivePoseEstimator odometry=new DifferentialDrivePoseEstimator(
	 /* Complex constructor parameters; not relevant*/
	)
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//Read the odometry object and set the pose. //Reference only
		field.setRobotPose(odometry.getPoseMeters());
		
		// Or, we can just set it manually for testing.
		field.setRobotPose(new Pose2d(2.7,3.1, new Rotation2d(Math.PI/2.0) ));	
	}
}

Now, when we open our Field2D widget in Glass, we'll see that our robot is at a new position. If we fully implemented our Pose Estimator object, we'd see that this provides realtime tracking of our position.

A .getRobotPose() also exists, but tends to be less useful in practice, as most classes that will interact with the Robot and Field will likely have access to the Odometry object directly.

Note, that the Field2d object we create is a unique reference, with it's own unique local data; only the NetworkTables key might have overlap when using default keys. This means if we want to properly share a Field across multiple classes, we either need to fetch the NetworkTables data and copy it over, create a single Field object in RobotContainer and pass it to, or create a DriverField object as a Singleton that can facilitate a single object.

Displaying Useful Targets

Where Field2d objects really shine is in adding supplemental information about other field objects. The utility varies by game, but it's great for showing a variety of things such as

  • Targets/objectives
  • Nearest/best target
  • Nearest game piece (detected by vision systems)

These can be done using the getObject(name) method; This grabs the named object from the field, creating it if it doesn't already exist.

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//Can provide any number of pose arguments
		field.getObject("GamePieces").setPoses(
			new Pose2d(1,1),
			new Pose2d(1,2),
			new Pose2d(1,3),
		);
		//You can also pass a single List<Pose2d> 
		//if you have a list of poses already
		
		field.getObject("BestGamePiece").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}

}

Note It's worth considering that for objects that never move, you could set objects once in the constructor, and they work fine. However, if the user accidentally moves them in the UI, it creates a visual mis-match between what the code is doing and what the user sees. As a result, it's often better to just throw it in a Periodic.

Field2d + User Input

A niche, but very useful application of field objects is to get precise driver feedback on field location data. This can be done using the following code setup:

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		//Set the pose  exactly once at boot
		field.getObject("DriverTarget").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}
	
	public Command aimAtCustomTarget(){
		return run(()->{
			var target=field.getObject("DriverTarget").getPose();
			//Do math to figure out the angle to target
			//Set your drivetrain to face the target
		};
	}
	
	public void periodic(){
		//No setting DriverTarget pose here!
	};
}

In this case, we take advantage of the "set once" approach in constructors; The drivers or programmers can modify the position, and then we now read it back into the code.

This can be very useful for testing to create "moving targets" to test dynamic behavior without having to drive the bot. It can also help you create "simulation" poses for testing math relating to Pose2D objects.

is especially true for simulation, as this allows you quickly test pose-related functions and makes sure that things happen how you expect.

One practical application is match-specific targets for cooperating with allies. An example is in 2024 Crescendo: a common game tactic was to "pass" rings across the field, by shooting to an open area near where your allies would be. However, since the game pieces can get stuck in/on robots, and different robots have different intakes, and each ally has different sight lines, making the ideal pass target unknown until the actual match is about to start. An adjustable target let the alliance sort it out before a match without having to change the code.

Displaying Paths

When doing path-planning for drivetrains, it's often helpful to display the full intended path, rather than a lot of individual poses. 

class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase{
	Field2D field = new Field();
	
	public Drivetrain(){//constructor
		SmartDashboard.putData("ChassisField",field);
		//Set the pose  exactly once at boot
		field.getObject("DriverTarget").setPose(
			new Pose2d(1,2)	
		);
	}
	
	public Command buildAuto1(){
		var  trajectory=// Get the trajectory object from your path tool
		field.getObject("autoTrajectory").setTrajectory(trajectory);
		return run(()->{
			//draw the rest of the owl
		};
	}
	

}

In this use case, the work will likely be done inside your Auto class after selecting the appropriate one.
